anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statements or transaction boundaries are written so they touch more rows, columns, or time than the business case requires.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Tables, indexes, partitions, and data types are laid out in a way that cannot satisfy the workload’s access patterns efficiently.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes consume an abnormally large share of CPU, driving the host to sustained saturation.

Composite definition: The composite anomaly represents the simultaneous presence of inefficient workload logic, a schema/index design that cannot serve the requested access patterns, and resulting CPU saturation. Poorly written queries meet a mismatched physical design, and the combined demand overwhelms compute resources.

Combined anomalous phenomena: Slow-query logs fill with recurring statements that show full-table scans or non-covering index probes; execution plans display wide scans, repeated lookups, and lack of partition pruning; host CPU utilization hovers near 100 %, with long OS run queues and scheduler wait events; statement latency forms a long tail, application timeouts and retries spike, and even well-written queries suffer from queueing delays. Monitoring may show sharp drops in throughput whenever a batch job or peak traffic window coincides with these conditions, and adding indexes or rewriting queries in isolation yields only partial relief.

Causal chain and interaction: Inefficient workload logic forces the engine to touch large data ranges. Because the schema lacks selective or covering indexes, these requests devolve into full scans and row-by-row lookups, multiplying CPU instructions per statement. The elevated CPU demand saturates the host, extending run-queue times and slowing plan compilation and context switching. CPU starvation, in turn, prolongs each already-inefficient query, causing longer transaction lifetimes, more contention, and additional retries that feed back into still higher CPU usage. Thus, the three root causes reinforce one another, creating a self-amplifying performance spiral that is harder to diagnose than any single issue alone.

entry.official_description: Statement violates GTID consistency: Updates to non-transactional tables can only be done in either autocommitted statements or single-statement transactions, and never in the same statement as updates to transactional tables.
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with unsupported syntax, invalid statement structure, or feature usage that the target engine version cannot execute as written.
entry.solution_guidance: Validate SQL syntax, target-engine compatibility, statement shape, and whether the feature is supported under the current engine version or execution context.
